planting.note: Scarify seed and sow in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy before spring growth; direct sow into lean, dry, sandy or gravelly soil since the taproot resents transplanting.

directions: Woolly locoweed forms a dense, silvery-haired mound of pinnately divided leaves on the shortgrass and black-grama plains of the southern High Plains and Chihuahuan Desert grassland, from the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles south through the Trans-Pecos and west into New Mexico. In early spring it sends up thick spikes of purple, lavender, or occasionally cream pea flowers held just above the foliage, blooming weeks before most other grassland forbs break dormancy. Caution: like other locoweeds, all parts contain swainsonine and are toxic to grazing livestock, so site it away from pastured animals and horse paddocks. Give it a lean, gravelly, unirrigated spot in full sun, since the deep taproot rots quickly in rich or consistently moist soil.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Plants of Texas Rangelands

planting.note: Nick or hot-water-scarify the hard seed coat and direct sow after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; germination is slow and uneven even with scarification.

directions: Twinleaf senna is a low, gray-green subshrub of open black-grama and tobosa grassland flats across the Trans-Pecos, southern New Mexico, and northern Mexico, easily told apart from other desert sennas by its leaves, which are reduced to just a single pair of rounded leaflets per stem. Loose clusters of one to three bright yellow flowers open along the stems through the warm season, drawing small native bees and serving as a larval host for sulphur butterflies. Hard frost kills the top growth back to the root crown most winters, but established plants resprout reliably from a woody base once soil warms in spring. It thrives on neglect in hot, caliche, or rocky soil and declines quickly if overwatered or planted in a rich garden bed.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has thoroughly warmed, since this frost-tender bunchgrass germinates poorly in cool soil; established clumps resprout each year from the crown even though top growth is killed back by hard freezes.

directions: Arizona cottontop is a warm-season bunchgrass of rocky hillsides, bajadas, and black-grama grassland flats across the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert borderlands, forming an upright clump of blue-green blades that flushes green quickly after summer rain. Its distinctive seed heads carry dense, soft, cottony-white hairs along the flower branches that catch morning light and give the whole plant a frosted look from late summer into fall. It is one of the more cold-tender of the Southwest's native grasses, with top growth dying back hard at the first freeze, but the crown survives and resprouts vigorously the following summer where winters are not severe. Plant it in full sun on fast-draining, rocky or gravelly ground and withhold irrigation once established, since wet feet in cool weather are its main cause of failure.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct sow into sandy to sandy-loam soil once it has warmed in late spring; this grass tolerates mildly saline ground and benefits from occasional runoff but needs sharp drainage overall.

directions: False Rhodes grass is a showy, blue-green bunchgrass of sandy draws, silty swales, and grassland flats across the Trans-Pecos, southern New Mexico, and Arizona, sending up airy flower stalks topped with several finger-like, feathery white seed branches reminiscent of its cultivated namesake Chloris gayana. It tolerates mildly saline and alkaline soils better than most companion grama grasses, making it a useful fit for the low, occasionally salty swales within an otherwise upland black-grama and tobosa grassland planting. Established clumps need no supplemental irrigation beyond natural rainfall and recover readily from drought once rooted. Cut back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge to keep the clump tidy and encourage the next season's full flush of seed heads.
sources: USDA NRCS E. "Kika" de la Garza Plant Materials Center

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; this compact bunchgrass establishes quickly from seed and needs no irrigation beyond occasional rain once rooted.

directions: Hall's panicgrass is a fine-textured, low bunchgrass scattered through rocky draws and open grassland flats from the Trans-Pecos and southern New Mexico into the Edwards Plateau, often growing in the thin gaps between black grama and tobosa tussocks rather than forming its own dense stands. Slender seed stalks rise just above the narrow blue-green foliage from spring through fall, maturing quickly and reseeding readily on bare, disturbed ground. Its smaller stature and tolerance of thin, rocky soil make it useful as a filler grass in a native grassland planting where taller bunchgrasses would otherwise leave bare gaps. It needs no fertilizer or supplemental water once established and holds up well to the thin caliche soils typical of its native range.
sources: USDA NRCS E. "Kika" de la Garza Plant Materials Center

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed into rocky or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; established tussocks tolerate heavy grazing and disturbance but need good drainage to persist.

directions: Spidergrass is a wiry, open-branched bunchgrass of rocky slopes, bajadas, and grassland flats throughout the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert borderlands, named for its widely spreading, spider-leg-like seed head branches that fan out well beyond the foliage clump. It greens up and flowers quickly in response to summer monsoon rain, then cures to a pale straw color that still holds seed value for grassland birds through the dry season. More tolerant of grazing and soil disturbance than many companion grama grasses, it often persists on compacted or heavily used ground where finer bunchgrasses thin out. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and expect essentially no maintenance once the deep root system is established.
sources: USDA NRCS Tucson Plant Materials Center Native Seed Vendor List
